text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Tax reform plans fail and financing of pension reform also endangered after ruling coalition and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) give up on attempts to reach a compromise.
- No new spelling rules for the moment in state of Hesse after local court upholds motion by father of two schoolchildren.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl visits flood-hit eastern Germany and calls aid operation a national task. Situation in the region remains critical, although no dikes broke overnight.
- Palestinian hijacker of a Lufthansa plane in 1977, sentenced last year to 12 years in prison, transferred at her own request from Hamburg to a Norwegian prison, where her husband and daughter live.
HANDELSBLATT

- Interest rises in the pipeline. If the dollar continues to climb strongly and the deutschemark weaken, the Bundesbank is ready to raise rates, according to the Handelsblatt interpretation of comments by central bank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick.
- Coalition plans for a grand tax reform seem to finally have failed.
- Chancellor Kohl assures flood victims of speedy government help on visit to region.
- Insurance group Allianz AG and Dresdner Bank AG announce deeper cooperation.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- Tax reform plans fail. Possibility of agreement in mediation committee as good as ruled out. Agreement on cutting supplementary wage costs also not expected. Special session of lower house of parliament called for Tuesday.
- Spelling reforms stopped in Hesse. Critics of the change in Bonn say ruling by the Hesse court means plans have failed.
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and International High Representative in Bosnia Carlos Westendorp call for complete clearing up of corruption charges against Bosnian politicians.
DIE WELT
- Fear of new breaks in dikes holding back swollen Oder river. Soldiers and volunteers still toiling to block threatened area of dike at Hohenwutzen.
- Spelling changes blocked in Hesse.
- Tax reform set to fail. Agreement seems only possible on cutting capital trading tax.
